title: 10 Classic Klaxons… Things to avoid doing or saying
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington lists ten common classroom habits he has watched teachers fall into repeatedly -- and admits to committing himself -- framing each as a moment that would trigger an imaginary game-show "klaxon." These include vague question stems that invite calling out rather than universal thinking ("Can anyone tell me..."), dead-end checks for understanding that produce a murmur but no real information, taking only one student's answer when thirty possible responses could have surfaced richer discussion, and "hanging a student out to dry" through an excruciating extended silence rather than simply providing the answer and moving on. He also flags banter during independent work time, teachers filling their own requested silence with extra instructions, giving only one worked example when a pattern requires at least two to become visible, assuming spoken explanation alone will "sink in" without practice, allowing no time for actual student practice after repeated demonstration, and reviewing test answers without ever surfacing why students got questions wrong. Sherrington frames the whole list as "things that make me cringe about my own teaching," prompted by watching other teachers, rather than a checklist aimed at anyone else, and closes by suggesting deliberate routines and norms for surfacing errors and misconceptions as the antidote to several of the ten patterns.
points: Sherrington's \"hanging a student out to dry\" klaxon describes a specific, painful classroom moment -- a student stuck in escalating silence on a question -- and recommends simply bailing them out and having the class rehearse the answer chorally instead.

His \"dead-end checks for understanding\" klaxon (\"does that make sense, yeah?\") names a widely used but functionally useless routine: a murmur or nod exchanges zero real information yet the teacher proceeds as if it did.

\"Giving only one example\" is flagged as a structural error, not a stylistic one: one example conflates the general pattern with its specific details, so a second, contrasting example is required for the pattern to become visible.

Sherrington explicitly frames the list as self-critique (\"I've done all of these things\") prompted by watching other teachers, rather than an external checklist -- a device meant to normalise admitting these habits rather than shame them.
quotes: I often imagine that classrooms could be wired with a QI studio wall klaxon that flashes and sounds an alarm when contestants say the obvious but wrong answer.

These checks are invariably met by a murmur or some nodding heads. Nobody says anything. Zero information is exchanged but the teacher takes it as a cue to proceed – often with undesirable consequences.
It's just not enough. The value of asking a follow-up question is huge especially when each answer has to take account of the previous one.
Hanging her out to dry just reinforces everyone’s sense that being unsure is a terrible thing to reveal. It’s a total own goal.
One example contains two sets of information: the general rule or pattern you want students to learn AND the specifics of that specific example. You can’t see a pattern from one thing.
If they don’t practice and consolidate- there’s not going to be much learning.
